LAYOFF AND REEMPLOYMENT RIGHTS OF CLASSIFIED (NON-CERTIFICATED) SCHOOL DISTRICT EMPLOYEES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Example Unified School District

CLASSIFIED SCHOOL EMPLOYEE LAYOFF — INFORMATION RECORD
CLASSIFIED SCHOOL EMPLOYEE LAYOFF — INFORMATION RECORD

School district: Example Unified School District
Classified employee: Jordan Lee
Job classification / position: Instructional Aide II
Date of hire: August 15, 2019
Stated effective date of layoff: June 30, 2027

This record accompanies the information that follows about the statutory scheme governing layoff and reemployment of classified (non-certificated) employees of California K-12 school districts under Education Code Part 25, Chapter 5. It states facts about that statutory scheme and about one published decision interpreting it; it does not determine whether the layoff described above complies with that scheme, and it is not a substitute for the district's own required notices.

THE STATUTORY SCHEME APPLIES WHETHER OR NOT THE DISTRICT HAS A MERIT SYSTEM
California school districts fall into two groups for purposes of classified-employee personnel administration: those that have adopted a merit system under Education Code Article 6 (administered by a personnel commission) and those that have not (where the governing board itself performs the personnel-administration functions). Education Code section 45114 addresses the second group directly: in a district without a personnel commission, the governing board may lay off and reemploy classified employees only by following the same procedures set out in sections 45298 and 45308 that a personnel commission would otherwise apply, with the statute itself substituting "governing board" for "personnel commission" wherever that phrase appears in those two sections. The layoff-order and reemployment rules described in the clauses below therefore apply to classified employees of merit-system and non-merit-system school districts alike.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "the governing board may lay off and reemploy classified employees only in accordance with procedures provided by Sections 45298 and 45308, except the term “personnel commission” therein shall be construed to mean the governing board."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45114 (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code, Part 25, Chapter 5, Article 1, layoff procedure in districts without a personnel commission (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45114.)
  Known gap: This document addresses only classified employees of K-12 school districts under Education Code Part 25 (the chapter these sections belong to). Classified employees of California community college districts are governed by separate statutory provisions elsewhere in the Education Code that this document has not researched and does not address. It also does not address how a particular position gets classified as "classified service" versus "certificated service" in the first place — that boundary determination is a distinct, and sometimes disputed, question this document does not cover.

LAYOFF FOR LACK OF WORK OR LACK OF FUNDS PROCEEDS BY LENGTH OF SERVICE
Education Code section 45308 states the basic rule for ordering a layoff of classified employees: classified employees are subject to layoff for lack of work or lack of funds, and when a layoff occurs, the order of layoff within a given class is fixed by length of service — not by discretionary selection. Within a class (and any higher classes bumped into as part of the same layoff), the employee with the shortest length of service is laid off first. When positions reopen, reemployment likewise proceeds in order of seniority, so the same length-of-service ranking that determines who is laid off first also determines who is recalled first.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "Classified employees shall be subject to layoff for lack of work or lack of funds. If a classified employee is laid off, the order of layoff within the class shall be determined by length of service. The employee who has been employed the shortest time in the class, plus higher classes, shall be laid off first. Reemployment shall be in order of seniority."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45308(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45308(a), classified employee layoff order by length of service (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45308.)
  Known gap: The statute states the ordering rule itself; it does not by itself resolve close seniority-date disputes (for example, disputes about which of two employees has the longer length of service where both were hired close in time) — those depend on the length-of-service computation rules in the separate clause below, and on facts about the individual district's records that this document has no way to verify.

HOW "LENGTH OF SERVICE" IS CALCULATED
Section 45308 also defines the "length of service" measure that the layoff-order rule depends on, and the definition is not the same for every district. For a school district with an average daily attendance below 250,000, length of service (for service on or after July 1, 1971) means all hours the employee was in paid status — whether during the school year, a holiday, a recess, or another period when school is in or out of session — but it excludes hours compensated solely on an overtime basis. A district's governing board may instead agree with the employees' exclusive representative to define length of service as the hire date, and may then extend that hire-date definition to a non-represented classification as well. A different rule applies to the state's very largest districts: for a school district with an average daily attendance of 250,000 or more, length of service for service on or after January 1, 1986 is determined by date of hire, not accumulated paid hours.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "in school districts with an average daily attendance below 250,000 for service commencing or continuing after July 1, 1971, “length of service” means all hours in paid status, whether during the school year, a holiday, recess, or during any period that a school is in session or closed, but does not include any hours compensated solely on an overtime basis as provided for in Section 45128."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45308(b)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45308(b)(1), definition of "length of service" for layoff purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45308.)
  Known gap: The 250,000-average-daily-attendance threshold as of this document's checked date effectively distinguishes one district (Los Angeles Unified) from the rest of the state, but this document has not independently verified any district's current average daily attendance figure, which can change from year to year and is a factual question this document does not research.

EFFECT OF UNPAID LEAVE ON SENIORITY CREDIT
Because length of service is normally counted by hours in paid status, an employee's time on unpaid leave could otherwise erode seniority standing. Section 45308 addresses this directly for several specific categories of unpaid leave: it does not preclude granting length-of-service credit for time spent on unpaid illness leave, unpaid maternity leave, unpaid family care leave, or unpaid industrial accident leave, and for a military leave of absence, length-of-service credit is instead granted under the separate rule in section 45297. Outside those named categories, the general rule reverses: if an employee returns to work after any other unpaid leave of absence, no further seniority accrues for the time the employee was not working.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "This section does not preclude the granting of “length of service” credit for time spent on unpaid illness leave, unpaid maternity leave, unpaid family care leave, or unpaid industrial accident leave. In addition, for military leave of absence, “length of service” credit shall be granted pursuant to Section 45297. In the event an employee returns to work following any other unpaid leave of absence, no further seniority shall be accrued for the time not worked."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45308(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45308(c), seniority credit for specified unpaid leaves (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45308.)
  Known gap: This clause does not independently research or quote Education Code section 45297's own military-leave credit mechanics; it states only that section 45308 defers to that separate section for military leave. It also does not attempt to classify every leave type a district might grant into one of these named categories versus the residual "other unpaid leave" category — that classification depends on the leave policy or leave statute actually at issue.

A LAID-OFF EMPLOYEE'S 39-MONTH REEMPLOYMENT RIGHTS
Layoff under this scheme is not necessarily a permanent severance of the employment relationship: Education Code section 45298 gives a person laid off for lack of work or lack of funds a 39-month period of reemployment eligibility. During that period, the person's reemployment takes preference over new applicants, and the person retains the right to participate in promotional examinations within the district. If the person is reemployed into a new position but does not complete the probationary period there, the statute does not simply end the person's reemployment eligibility — it returns the person to the reemployment list for whatever time remains of the original 39-month period, calculated from the date of that reemployment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "A person laid off because of lack of work or lack of funds shall be eligible for reemployment for a period of 39 months as follows:(1) The person’s reemployment shall take preference over new applicants.(2) The person shall have the right to participate in promotional examinations within the district during the period of 39 months."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45298(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45298(a), 39-month reemployment eligibility after layoff (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45298.)
  Known gap: This clause covers only the reemployment-list mechanics themselves. It does not address how a district maintains or is required to notify laid-off employees of vacancies against that list, which is an operational and recordkeeping question this document has not researched.

VOLUNTARY DEMOTION IN LIEU OF LAYOFF CARRIES THE SAME REEMPLOYMENT RIGHTS
Section 45298 extends comparable protection to an employee who accepts a voluntary demotion or a voluntary reduction in assigned time — either in lieu of being laid off outright, or to remain in a current position rather than be reclassified or reassigned. That employee is granted the same rights as a person who was actually laid off, and in addition retains eligibility to be considered for reemployment for up to 24 additional months beyond what a straightforward layoff would provide, provided the employee still meets the same tests of fitness under which the employee originally qualified for appointment to the class. The statute assigns the personnel commission the job of setting the specific eligibility period on a class-by-class basis, and separately gives an employee who took a voluntary demotion or reduction the option to be returned to a position in the former class, or to a position with increased assigned time, as vacancies open up — without any outer time limit, though subject to proper seniority ranking on a valid reemployment list if one exists.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "An employee who takes a voluntary demotion or a voluntary reduction in assigned time in lieu of layoff or to remain in his or her present position rather than be reclassified or reassigned, shall be granted the same rights as persons laid off and shall retain eligibility to be considered for reemployment for an additional period of up to 24 months, provided that the same tests of fitness under which the employee qualified for appointment to the class still apply."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45298(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45298(b), voluntary demotion or reduction in lieu of layoff (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45298.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the voluntary-demotion-in-lieu-of-layoff mechanism as section 45298 states it; it does not address how a district must document that an employee's demotion was in fact voluntary, which is a factual and evidentiary question this document does not resolve.

THE ANNUAL LAYOFF NOTICE PROCESS AND THE RIGHT TO REQUEST A HEARING
For a layoff tied to the ensuing school year, Education Code section 45117 layers a notice-and-hearing process on top of the seniority rules above. No later than March 15, and before the governing board actually gives a classified employee notice that the employee's services will not be required for the ensuing year due to lack of work or lack of funds, the school district's superintendent (or the superintendent's designee, or, in a district without a superintendent, the clerk or secretary of the governing board) must give the governing board and the employee written notice that this recommendation has been made, stating the reasons and informing the employee of the employee's displacement rights, if any, and reemployment rights. Once that recommendation notice is given, the classified employee may request a hearing on whether cause exists for not reemploying the employee for the ensuing year. The request must be in writing, delivered to whoever sent the notice, by a deadline the notice itself must specify — a deadline that cannot be set less than seven days after the employee was served with the notice. An employee who does not request a hearing by that deadline waives the right to one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "before a classified employee is given notice by the governing board of a school district that the employee’s services will not be required for the ensuing year due to lack of work or lack of funds, the governing board of the school district and the employee shall be given written notice by the superintendent of the school district or the superintendent’s designee, or, in the case of a school district that has no superintendent, by the clerk or secretary of the governing board of the school district, that it has been recommended that the notice be given to the employee, stating the reasons that the employee’s services will not be required for the ensuing year, and informing the employee of the employee’s displacement rights, if any, and reemployment rights."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45117(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45117(a), March 15 recommendation-notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45117.)
  "A classified employee may request a hearing to determine if there is cause for not reemploying the employee for the ensuing year. A request for a hearing shall be in writing and shall be delivered to the person who sent the notice, on or before a date specified in subdivision (a), which shall not be less than seven days after the date on which the notice is served upon the employee."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45117(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45117(b), employee's right to request a hearing and the 7-day minimum deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45117.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the March-15-anchored process for a layoff effective at the start of the ensuing school year. It does not address whether or how a mid-year layoff (one not tied to the annual reduction-in-force cycle this section describes) triggers the same notice-and-hearing sequence, which this document has not separately researched.

THE HEARING ITSELF, AND WHY THE RESULT DIFFERS FROM A CERTIFICATED TEACHER'S DISMISSAL HEARING
If a hearing is requested, section 45117 routes it through the state's general administrative adjudication procedure (Government Code section 11500 et seq.), with the school district's governing board holding the powers of the agency in that framework, subject to several district-specific rules the statute lays out — including short deadlines for the employee's notice of participation and for requesting discovery, and a requirement that the hearing be conducted by an administrative law judge. Critically, though, the outcome of that hearing is advisory rather than binding: the administrative law judge prepares a proposed decision containing findings of fact and a recommendation, but the governing board of the school district makes the final determination as to the sufficiency of the cause and disposition, and none of the administrative law judge's findings, recommendations, or determinations bind the board. The statute also clarifies what "cause" means in this context: for purposes of this section, cause for layoff includes the district's compliance with the seniority requirements described elsewhere in the Education Code, including section 45308.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "the governing board of the school district shall make the final determination as to the sufficiency of the cause and disposition. None of the findings, recommendations, or determinations contained in the proposed decision prepared by the administrative law judge shall be binding on the governing board of the school district."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45117(c)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45117(c)(3)(A), governing board makes the final, non-binding determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45117.)
  "For purposes of this section, “cause” for layoff includes school district compliance with the seniority requirements of this code, including Section 45308."
  — Cal. Educ. Code § 45117(c)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Education Code § 45117(c)(3)(B), "cause" defined as compliance with seniority requirements including § 45308 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=45117.)
  Known gap: This non-binding structure is a meaningful point of contrast with this corpus's separate document on certificated (tenured teacher) dismissal, where the Commission on Professional Competence's decision is binding rather than merely advisory to the governing board — a classified employee's hearing right under section 45117 does not carry that same binding effect. This clause also does not research the deadline and expense provisions of section 45117(c)(1)-(2) and (3)(A) beyond what is quoted here, including the specific notice-of-participation and discovery deadlines, the May 7 proposed-decision delivery date, or the May 15 termination-notice deadline.

A LAYOFF PRESENTED AS "LACK OF FUNDS" CAN STILL BE UNLAWFUL IF AN IMPERMISSIBLE REASON WAS A BUT-FOR CAUSE
In Short v. Nevada Joint Union High School District (1985) 163 Cal.App.3d 1087, a California Court of Appeal addressed a classified employee's claim that a school district's elimination of his position — presented as a budget-driven layoff — was in substantial part a pretext to remove him for reasons unrelated to the budget. The court held that the employee's evidence was sufficient to establish a prima facie case of what it called a "dual motive" termination, where both a permissible reason (the budget) and an impermissible reason contributed to the district's decision. The court's rule for resolving such a case placed the ultimate burden on the district: a district's decision is unlawful if it would not have been made but for the impermissible reason, and once the employee establishes a prima facie dual-motive case, the burden of persuasion shifts to the district to prove the decision would have been made even without the impermissible reason.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-08]
  "We hold that the District’s decision is unlawful if it would not have been made but for impermissible reasons. We hold further that once plaintiff established his prima facie case, the burden of persuasion shifted to the District to prove the decision would have been made even in the absence of impermissible reasons."
  — Short v. Nevada Joint Union High School District, 163 Cal. App. 3d 1087, 210 Cal. Rptr. 297 (1985) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2139573/short-v-nevada-joint-union-high-school-district/)
  Known gap: This decision predates the current text of Education Code section 45117 quoted elsewhere in this document — the opinion describes a version of section 45117 that required 30 days' advance notice of layoff, a provision not present in the section's current text, which instead centers on the March 15/May 15 annual cycle described above. This document has not researched what, if anything, in the amended statute now serves the same notice-timing function the court referenced, nor whether the dual-motive framework the court announced has been applied, narrowed, or extended by any later published decision.

CLOSING
This information record was prepared regarding the classified employee, school district, and stated layoff effective date identified at the top of this document.

City/state: Sacramento, California
Date: September 8, 2026

This document states facts about the statutory scheme described above and about one published decision interpreting it. It does not determine whether any particular layoff complies with that scheme, and it does not recommend any course of action to the employee, the school district, or any other reader.

expectedJSON.body: If a hearing is requested, section 45117 routes it through the state's general administrative adjudication procedure (Government Code section 11500 et seq.), with the school district's governing board holding the powers of the agency in that framework, subject to several district-specific rules the statute lays out — including short deadlines for the employee's notice of participation and for requesting discovery, and a requirement that the hearing be conducted by an administrative law judge. Critically, though, the outcome of that hearing is advisory rather than binding: the administrative law judge prepares a proposed decision containing findings of fact and a recommendation, but the governing board of the school district makes the final determination as to the sufficiency of the cause and disposition, and none of the administrative law judge's findings, recommendations, or determinations bind the board. The statute also clarifies what "cause" means in this context: for purposes of this section, cause for layoff includes the district's compliance with the seniority requirements described elsewhere in the Education Code, including section 45308.

citations.cite: California Education Code § 45117(c)(3)(A), governing board makes the final, non-binding determination
citations.quote: the governing board of the school district shall make the final determination as to the sufficiency of the cause and disposition. None of the findings, recommendations, or determinations contained in the proposed decision prepared by the administrative law judge shall be binding on the governing board of the school district.

expectedJSON.gap: This non-binding structure is a meaningful point of contrast with this corpus's separate document on certificated (tenured teacher) dismissal, where the Commission on Professional Competence's decision is binding rather than merely advisory to the governing board — a classified employee's hearing right under section 45117 does not carry that same binding effect. This clause also does not research the deadline and expense provisions of section 45117(c)(1)-(2) and (3)(A) beyond what is quoted here, including the specific notice-of-participation and discovery deadlines, the May 7 proposed-decision delivery date, or the May 15 termination-notice deadline.

expectedJSON.body: In Short v. Nevada Joint Union High School District (1985) 163 Cal.App.3d 1087, a California Court of Appeal addressed a classified employee's claim that a school district's elimination of his position — presented as a budget-driven layoff — was in substantial part a pretext to remove him for reasons unrelated to the budget. The court held that the employee's evidence was sufficient to establish a prima facie case of what it called a "dual motive" termination, where both a permissible reason (the budget) and an impermissible reason contributed to the district's decision. The court's rule for resolving such a case placed the ultimate burden on the district: a district's decision is unlawful if it would not have been made but for the impermissible reason, and once the employee establishes a prima facie dual-motive case, the burden of persuasion shifts to the district to prove the decision would have been made even without the impermissible reason.

citations.case: Short v. Nevada Joint Union High School District
citations.quote: We hold that the District’s decision is unlawful if it would not have been made but for impermissible reasons. We hold further that once plaintiff established his prima facie case, the burden of persuasion shifted to the District to prove the decision would have been made even in the absence of impermissible reasons.

expectedJSON.gap: This decision predates the current text of Education Code section 45117 quoted elsewhere in this document — the opinion describes a version of section 45117 that required 30 days' advance notice of layoff, a provision not present in the section's current text, which instead centers on the March 15/May 15 annual cycle described above. This document has not researched what, if anything, in the amended statute now serves the same notice-timing function the court referenced, nor whether the dual-motive framework the court announced has been applied, narrowed, or extended by any later published decision.
